text: over 2,000 years ago the Roman Empire was ruled by an extraordinary Emperor whose story reads like the pages of an Epic Novel this was Marcus Aurelius not merely a ruler of vast territories but a philosopher king whose profound wisdom and Serene demeanor set him apart in a time of brutal conquests and Palace intrigues imagine a leader who wielded not just the sword but the power of stoic philosophy guiding his Empire with both might and mind his Reign was marked by an aura of respect so intense that both allies and adversaries Look to Him with reverence in today's world where chaos often Reigns and respect can be hard to earn the lessons from Marcus Aurelius are not just historical footnotes but essential tools for anyone looking to stand out as a leader or simply be more influential in their daily interactions this video will delve into eight specific strategies inspired by Marcus himself that can dramatically enhance how you command respect transforming not only how others perceive you but how you perceive yourself I have personally woven these ancient strategies into the fabric of my everyday life experiencing firsthand their power to change the Dynamics of interactions at work and in personal relationships these are not just theories they are practical actions that can lead to real and profound changes in your life get ready to embark on a journey back in time that will equip you for a better tomorrow whether you're looking to lead with more Authority maintain Poise in challenging situations or simply Inspire more admiration among your peers the wisdom of Marcus Aurelius has the answers let's unlock these secrets together and step into a world where respect is not demanded but effortlessly attracted number one Embrace calm movements in the world of constant hustle where everything demands urgency slowing down might seem counterintuitive yet there lies profound strength in the deliberate calmness of our actions this notion is deeply rooted in stoic philosophy which teaches us that the control over our movements ref FS Mastery over our minds a true sign of wisdom and composure When You observe individuals who are highly respected and carry an aura of authority you'll often notice their movements are measured and intentional consider a seasoned chess player who thoughtfully touches each piece contemplating their next move with a cool demeanor their calm isn't just a show of confidence in their strategy it's a tactic to unsettle opponents projecting an image of unwavering control similarly When leaders whether in boardrooms at public speaking events or even in casual social settings move with poise they command attention and respect effortlessly this isn't about mimicking slow motion but rather embracing a pace that allows you to remain aware and present in every situation it's the difference between reacting impulsively under stress and responding with thoughtfulness the slow assured handshake of a business leader meeting a new client sends a silent message of confidence and builds trust more effectively Than A hurried distracted interaction could the power of calm movements extends Beyond just physical motions it influences our mental responses for example during negotiations those who take a moment to pause and consider their responses are often seen as more credible and composed this reflects the stoic practice of withholding immediate reactions which allows for better decision making and displays a level of sophistication in handling complex interactions now integrating this into your daily life doesn't require Monumental changes it starts with small everyday interactions next time you find yourself in a stressful situation try consciously slowing down your movements if you're running late instead of letting Panic dictate your actions take a deep breath and maintain your usual Pace this helps in maintaining a clear head to think about the best course of action without letting stress take over the effects of such changes are more profound than one might assume they not only enhance how others perceive rece you but also improve your own self-regulation a core component of stoic Philosophy by controlling your external movements you are subtly training your mind to manage your internal emotional states this doesn't mean suppressing emotions but understanding and channeling them through a filter of calm and control in a world that often equates busyness with productivity and worth choosing calm and deliberate actions is a powerful stance it sets you apart as someone who is not easily overwhelmed and who values quality and mindfulness in their actions traits that naturally draw respect and admiration so as we navigate through our fast-paced lives let's remind ourselves of the wisdom in calmness by embracing this stoic practice we not only enhance our interactions with the world around us but also cultivate a Serene in inner world this dual impact enriches Our Lives making us not just respected figures but also balanced and happy individuals remember the calmest person in the room is often the one who has the most control not just over themselves but often over the outcome of situations number two maintain steady eye contact eye contact is like a silent conversation an unspoken exchange that says Much More Than Words often do it's a fundamental element of effective communication fostering connection and understanding between individuals while the eyes are often termed the windows to the soul in the context of leadership and respect they could well be considered the doors to trust and influence think about when you're engaged in a casual chat with a friend or discussing a critical business matter the moments where you lock eyes tend to be those where you feel feel most heard and valued this isn't coincidental but a testament to the power of eye contact in human interactions maintaining steady eye contact signifies that you are fully present and invested in the interaction which naturally encourages the other person to reciprocate with equal attention and respect this practice aligns closely with stoic principles that emphasize mindfulness and Presence by maintaining eye contact you are practicing external control which reflects an internal state of focus and calm it's about being fully in the moment an essential trait for anyone looking to lead or influence effectively stoicism teaches us to focus on what we can control and how we engage with others through our gaze is certainly a powerful tool at our disposal let's illustrate this with a common scenario imagine you're at a working event the room is buzzing with conversations and you're introduced to a potential key contact as you discuss possible collaborations maintaining steady calm eye contact can set you apart from others who may glance away check their phones or look over shoulders for the next handshake such undivided attention can make the person feel respected and valued laying the groundwork for a strong professional relationship moreover steady eye contact is not just about professional settings it plays a crucial role in personal relationships too when family members or friends are discussing something close to their hearts looking them in the eyes as they speak can make them feel supported and understood it's a simple yet profound way to strengthen bonds and show that you care however it's important to remember that effective eye contact is not about about staring intently without break which can come off as aggressive or uncomfortable instead it's about finding a balance where your gaze is steady but gentle assertive yet inviting it involves occasionally breaking eye contact in a natural thoughtful manner to keep the interaction comfortable and positive integrating steady eye contact into your daily interactions also enhances your ability to read and respond to nonverbal C use often a person's eyes can communicate much about their feelings and reactions which words might not fully capture by paying attention to these subtle signals you can respond more empathetically and effectively aligning your words and actions with the needs and emotions of the conversation number three stay nonreactive in conflict conflict is an inevitable part of life but how you respond to it defines your character and determines the outcome staying calm and non-reactive during these moments isn't about suppressing emotions or appearing indifferent it's about choosing a response that aligns with your values and serves a constructive purpose the stoics believed that while we can't control the actions or words of others we can absolutely control how we react to them think about a time when someone raised Ed their voice at you perhaps in a heated disagreement or during a moment of frustration the instinctive reaction might have been to raise your voice back or lash out defensively but what if instead you paused took a breath and responded in a measured tone the shift in Dynamics is almost immediate by refusing to match the other person's emotional intensity you deescalate the situation and regain control of the inter action this ability to remain non-reactive in Conflict requires practice and self-awareness both Central to stoic philosophy the stoics often spoke of imagining yourself as a rock in the sea a steadfast presence that remains unmoved no matter how turbulent the waves around it become when you adopt this mindset you become someone who cannot be easily provoked or swayed earning respect and Authority in the eyes of of others one practical way to cultivate non-reactivity is to remind yourself that the actions or words of others are not personal they're often a reflection of their own struggles emotions or perceptions for instance if a colleague criticizes your work in an unkind way it's easy to feel attacked but pausing to recognize that their words may stem from stress or insecurity allows you to respond with Clarity and professionalism rather than defensiveness another example could be in personal relationships imagine a partner or close friend says something hurtful during an argument reacting impulsively might escalate the conflict potentially leading to words or actions you later regret however choosing to step back both physically and emotionally gives you the space to reflect and respond with empathy a calm response like I understand you're upset let's talk about this when we're both Karma can redirect the conversation toward resolution rather than further division the stoics also advocated for the practice of perspective ask yourself will this matter in a week a month a year this simple question can often diffuse the intensity of the moment helping you prioritize what truly deserves your energy and attention many conflicts that seem significant In the Heat of the Moment lose their power when viewed through the lens of time staying non-reactive doesn't mean being passive or avoiding confrontation it's about engaging with conflict thoughtfully and strategically when you maintain your composure you set the tone for the interaction demonstrating leadership and emotional intelligence this approach not only resolves conflicts more effectively but also enhances how others perceive you as someone who is capable grounded and wise number four adapt to your audience every interaction is a unique opportunity to connect with others and the key to making those connections meaningful lies in understanding your audience whether you're addressing a large crowd having a one-on-one conversation or simply sharing ideas in a team meeting tailoring your approach to fit the people in front of you is one of the most effective ways to build respect and trust this is not about being inauthentic it's about meeting people where they are to ensure your message resonates imagine being at a family gathering where you're discussing an important topic if you use technical jargon or overly formal language your relatives might tune out or feel alienated but if you simplify your ideas and relate them to Shared experiences or family values they're more likely to engage and respond positively the ability to adjust how you communicate based on who you're speaking to is a skill that can transform not just conversations but relationships the stoics understood the importance of empathy and practicality in communication they emphasize the need to listen actively and observe others to better understand their persp perspective for example if you're mentoring a new team member at work take time to learn about their background and experience level if they're new to the field break Concepts down into simpler terms and encourage questions on the other hand if you're discussing the same topic with a seasoned expert you might dive deeper into technical details and focus on collaboration rather than instruction a great way to practice adapting to your audience is by observing their body language and tone are they nodding along or looking confused are they leaning into listen or glancing around the room these subtle cues can give you immediate feedback about how your message is being received allowing you to adjust in real time for instance if someone seems disengaged asking a question like does this make sense to you or what are your thoughts on this so far can help re-engage them in public speaking this principle becomes even more critical addressing a group of students for example might require using stories and relatable examples to keep their attention while a presentation to senior Executives may call for concise datadriven insights the content doesn't change in essence but how you frame it does ensuring it lands effectively with your audience one of the most important aspects of adapting to your audience is recognizing that it's not just about what you say but how you say it a calm friendly tone might work well in a casual conversation but a firmer more authoritative tone might be necessary when addressing a team during a crisis the stoics believed in observing and reflecting on the needs of the moment and responding accordingly a principle that remains Timeless even in challenging situations such as disagreements or negotiations adapting to your audience can be a GameChanger let's say you're in a heated debate with a colleague if they're speaking emotionally responding with cold logic might escalate the tension instead acknowledging their feelings with a phrase like I can see this is really important to you can diffuse the intensity and create space for a more productive discussion adapt to your audience is not about being manipulative it's about respecting others enough to communicate in ways that resonate with them this approach Fosters trust reduces misunderstandings and strengthens your ability to influence and Inspire by practicing this stoic inspired principle you demonstrate not only emotional intelligence but also a commitment to fostering meaningful and respectful connections over over time this adaptability becomes second nature empowering you to navigate diverse interactions with Grace and Effectiveness number five speak with conviction when you speak your words carry weight but how much weight depends largely on the conviction behind them conviction is not just about volume or passion it's about speaking with certainty Clarity and an unshakable belief in what you're saying it's the difference between someone hesitantly suggesting an idea and someone confidently declaring this is the way forward people are naturally drawn to confidence because it signals competence and trustworthiness think about a time when someone spoke with conviction and how it made you feel maybe it was a teacher explaining a complex concept or a friend sharing a bold idea they were passionate about their confidence likely inspired you to believe in their message even if you weren't entirely sure at first that's the power of conviction it not only makes your words more impactful but also influences how others perceive and respond to you the stoics understood this deeply they believed in speaking only when necessary and ensuring that their words were grounded in truth and reason if you think about it conviction often comes from preparation and clarity when you're clear about what you stand for your words naturally carry more power for example imagine you're pitching a project at work instead of saying I think this could be a good idea try saying this is the solution that will achieve our goals that slight shift in tone and phrasing changes how your message is received it moves from possibility to certainty which is much harder to ignore speaking with conviction doesn't mean shutting down dialogue or being inflexible it's about presenting your ideas with confidence while remaining open to other perspectives if someone challenges your Viewpoint listen thoughtfully and respond with the same assured tone for instance if a colleague says I'm not sure this will work a response like I hear your concerns but here's why this approach is effective shows both confidence and respect another key aspect of speaking with conviction is your body language and tone even the most well-thought out words can lose their impact if delivered with hesitation or uncertainty practice speaking in a steady calm voice with a slight downward inflection at the end of your sentences this signals Authority and finality pair that with confident posture Standing Tall maintaining steady eye contact and using purposeful gestures and your words will resonate even more let's not forget that conviction isn't just for formal settings it plays a crucial role in everyday interactions as well for example if a friend asks for advice and you respond with hesitation they might doubt your suggestion but if you reply with confidence even a simple statement like I think this is the best choice for you can provide reassurance and Clarity stoicism teaches us that conviction comes from aligning our words with our principles when you truly believe in what you're saying it shows your authenticity shines through making it easier for others to trust and respect you this is why self-reflection is so important the more you understand your values and priorities the more naturally conviction will flow into your speech in a world where so many voices compete for attention speaking with conviction is a powerful way to stand out it's not about being the loudest or the most aggressive it's about being clear confident and unwavering in your message whether you're leading a meeting sharing your ideas or simply offering a kind word let your conviction show it's not just about being heard it's about being remembered and respected number six use confident tones there's something undeniably magnetic about the way someone speaks when their tone carries confidence it's not just about what's being said but how it's delivered that makes all the difference a confident tone is steady deliberate and reassuring signaling to your audience that you know what you're talking about and believe in it fully it's a skill that anyone can cultivate and when you do it changes the way people perceive and respond to you picture this you're explaining an idea to a group and your voice wavers slightly trailing off at the end of sentences even if your idea is brilliant the lack of certainty in your tone can make others question it now imagine delivering the same idea with a calm clear voice maintaining an even volume and finishing each sentence with conviction it doesn't just sound better it feels more trustworthy people naturally gravitate towards those who seem assured because it inspires confidence in them as well the stoics valued control over the self and that includes how we communicate they believed in tempering emotions ensuring that words were spoken with Clarity and purpose a confident tone reflects this control it shows that you're not ruled by doubt or anxiety but are instead grounded Ed in your message this doesn't mean you need to be loud or forceful confidence often lies in subtlety a measured steady tone can carry more weight than a raised voice ever could let's take a common scenario giving feedback if you're speaking to a colleague about something they need to improve using a hesitant tone can undermine your message they might focus more on your uncertainty than the feedback itself on the other hand delivering the same message with a balanced tone firm but not harsh conveys both Authority and care for example saying I believe you can improve in this area and here's how I think you can do it with a steady voice shows that you're invested in their growth not just pointing out flaws tone also plays a huge role in conflict resolution imagine two people arguing their voices Rising as they try to outshout each other now picture someone stepping into that situation with a calm confident tone saying let's take a moment to listen to each other that single statement can shift the energy of the conversation entirely confidence in tone isn't just about asserting yourself it's also about bringing calm and control to chaotic situations even in personal settings the way you use your tone can make a big difference think about comforting a friend who's going through a tough time if you speak softly but with steady Assurance saying something like you're going to get through this and I'm here to support you your tone alone can offer a sense of stability and hope to develop a confident tone start by slowing down your speech rushing through words often makes you sound unsure pausing between key points not only gives your audience time to absorb your message but also projects calmness practice lowering your voice slightly at the end of sentences which conveys certainty and finality pay attention to your breathing as well a steady Rhythm helps maintain a composed tone even Under Pressure confidence in tone is about more than just sounding good it's about embodying a sense of control and intention it reflects your inner state aligning perfectly with the stoic ideal of self-mastery when you speak with a confident tone you're not just sharing information you're inviting trust fostering respect and creating a space where your words can truly resonate it's a skill that takes practice but yields incredible results transforming not just how others hear you but how they remember and regard you number seven utilize pauses if effectively silence when used intentionally can be just as powerful as words in fact pauses in conversation or speech often have a greater impact than we realize a pause gives your audience time to reflect process and anticipate what's coming next it's a skillful tool that adds depth to your communication making your words carry more weight in stoic philosophy the practice of measured thought and deliberate action is highly emphasized and this applies beautifully to how we use pauses in our conversations think about a great Storyteller they don't rush through their Tales instead they pause at Key moments just before revealing an exciting twist or delivering an important lesson that brief silence builds anticipation and draws The Listener in making the moment more memorable you can apply this same principle in your every day interactions whether you're explaining an idea making a point in a meeting or even telling a joke a well-placed pause can enhance the impact of your message in conversations pauses can also convey confidence if someone asks you a challenging question taking a moment before you answer shows that you're thoughtful and composed not rattled or defensive contrast that with rushing to respond without thinking which might come across as un certain or even careless a pause says I'm considering this carefully because it matters pauses aren't just about giving others time to absorb your words they're also about giving yourself time to reflect imagine you're in a debate or negotiation and the discussion is becoming heated instead of jumping in with a quick retort take a breath pause and then respond that brief moment can help you choose your words more carefully ensuring your response aligns with your goals and values this practice mirrors the stoic approach of responding to situations with reason and control rather than impulsivity even in public speaking where silence might feel awkward pauses are invaluable for example after stating a critical point pause for a couple of seconds let's say you're presenting a strategy to your team this plan will not only save us time pause it will also increase our efficiency by 30% that moment of silence emphasizes the importance of what you just said giving it a chance to sink in pauses can also signal that you're actively listening when someone finishes speaking resisting the urge to immediately jump in with your response shows respect for their words a brief pause before replying demonstrates that you're taking the time to consider their perspective fostering trust and mutual understanding even in storytelling or casual conversations pauses can create more engaging interactions picture telling a story to a group of friends and then just as we thought the hike couldn't get any worse pause we heard the sound of thunder that moment of silence heightens the suspense pulling your audience deeper into the experience it's a small technique but incredibly effective in keeping people invested practicing the art of the pause requires patience and self-awareness in today's fast-paced world where conversations often feel like a race to see who can speak the most intentionally slowing down can feel unnatural at first but the benefits are worth it pauses allow you to communicate with Clarity intention and impact all qualities of a confident and thoughtful speaker number eight leverage influence wisely influence is a tool and like any tool its impact depends on how it's used it can build Bridges or burn them Inspire others or manipulate them using influence wisely isn't just about getting others to do what you want it's about fostering respect trust and and positive outcomes for everyone involved the stoics believed in the principle of leading by example and acting in harmony with reason and virtue making wise influence a Cornerstone of their philosophy imagine you're in a leadership role at work you have the authority to delegate tasks and make decisions now you could demand that your team follows orders without question but what does that achieve likely resentment or or compliance without real engagement on the other hand if you use your influence to inspire collaboration explaining why certain tasks are critical seeking input and recognizing contributions you create an environment where people feel valued and motivated your influence then becomes a force for Unity and productivity consider a mentor mentee relationship a mentor holds significant influence over their men personal and professional growth when a mentor uses that influence to guide with encouragement and constructive feedback it empowers the mentee to grow and achieve their potential this reflects the stoic idea of acting with the greater good in mind using influence not to control but to elevate others stoicism teaches us to focus on what we can control and influence Falls firmly within that realm you can't control how others react but you can control how you present your ideas and how you lead by example for instance if you're trying to encourage sustainable practices in your community you'll likely have more success showing how you've implemented those practices in your own life than simply telling others what to do people respect action over words and influence is most effective when it's rooted in authenticity let's also talk about without influence in moments of conflict when emotions are high the temptation to dominate the conversation or force a resolution can be strong but leveraging influence wisely means taking a step back listening to all sides and guiding the discussion toward a constructive outcome for example in a disagreement with a friend calmly stating I want to understand your perspective better before we move forward can deescalate intentions and demonstrate your commitment to the relationship this approach not only resolves the immediate conflict but also strengthens the bond of mutual respect another dimension of influence is understanding its ripple effect every decision you make every action you take has the potential to impact others far beyond the immediate situation if you're a parent the way you handle challenges and interact with others becomes a blueprint for your children if you're a manager your attitude toward challenges sets the tone for your team this awareness is vital to using influence responsibly and ethically wisely leveraging influence also involves text: Born in 1889 into one of Europe's wealthiest families, Vitkinstein seemed destined for engineering. Instead, he became arguably the most influential philosopher of the 20th century. His impact reaches far beyond academic philosophy, touching linguistics, cognitive science, artificial intelligence, mathematics, psychology, and even how we think about art and religion. But here is what makes Vitkinstein truly different. Most philosophers build grand systems and defend them for life. Vitkinstein built a system so elegant it claimed to solve all philosophical problems, then spent the rest of his life showing why that entire approach was fundamentally mistaken. His work centers on one deceptively simple question. What is the relationship between language, thought, and reality? This might sound abstract, but consider this. Every argument you have ever had, every misunderstanding, every confusion about what something means, every philosophical puzzle, every scientific theory traces back to this relationship. If we get language wrong, we get everything wrong. We begin with the early Vitkinstein and a book he believed ended philosophy forever. Part one, the tractatus and the picture theory. When Vitkinstein thought he solved philosophy in 1921, 3 years after completing the manuscript while a prisoner of war, Vitkinstein published a slim book of just 75 pages. The Tractatus lojiko philosophicus is one of the most cryptic and influential works in western philosophy. He genuinely believed this book had solved all philosophical problems that could be solved. Everything else, he thought, was just confusion about language. The book opens with seven main propositions, each numbered with subpropositions that drill deeper. This mathematical structure was not decoration. It reflected Vitkinstein's belief that philosophy should have the precision of logic. Let me give you the beating heart of the tractatus. Vitkinstein proposed what philosophers call the picture theory of language. Here is the core idea. Language works by picturing reality. Think about a photograph. A photograph represents a scene because the arrangement of elements in the photo corresponds to the arrangement of elements in reality. If there is a tree to the left of a house in reality, the photo shows this same spatial relationship. Vitkinstein argued that meaningful sentences work exactly the same way. Take the sentence, the cat is on the mat. For this sentence to be meaningful, it must picture a possible state of affairs. The structure of the sentence with cat related to Matt by on mirrors the structure of reality where a cat relates to a mat by being on top of it. The sentence shares a logical form with the fact it represents. This seems simple, but the implications are staggering. First, Vitkinstein concluded that the world consists of facts, not things. The world is not a collection of objects floating around. It is the totality of facts, of states of affairs that obtain. The cat is on the mat is not about two separate objects, but about a fact, a configuration of reality. Second, for language to picture reality, there must be something language and reality share, logical form. This is not something we can say directly, Vitkinstein argued. It shows itself. You cannot step outside language to describe how language relates to reality because any such description would itself be in language. Logical form is the limit of what can be said. Third, and this is where it gets radical, any sentence that cannot picture a possible state of affairs is literally nonsense. Not false, not wrong, but meaningless. Consider the sentence, the number seven is green. This does not picture any possible state of affairs. Numbers cannot have colors in the way the sentence suggests or take goodness is above evil. Where exactly in what space? The sentence has grammatical form but no logical form corresponding to reality. And here is the devastating conclusion Vitkinstein drew. Most of philosophy consists of sentences that look grammatically correct but picture nothing. Questions like, "What is the meaning of being?" or "Does the soul exist?" or "Is beauty objective?" cannot be answered because they cannot be asked properly. They are pseudo questions arising from misunderstanding how language works. Let me give you a concrete example that shows why this theory seems so powerful. Consider the philosophical debate about whether universals exist. Plato argued that when we call multiple things red, there must be an abstract form of redness that exists independently. Nomalists argued that only particular red things exist and redness is just a name we use. Vitkinstein would say this entire debate is confused. The sentence redness exists does not picture any state of affairs. You cannot point to where redness is the way you can point to a red apple. The debate arises because we mistake grammatical form for logical form. We think because redness is a noun like apple. It must refer to something the way Apple does. But this is a language trap. The implications cascaded through every area of philosophy. Ethics. Vitkinstein argued that ethical statements cannot picture facts about the world. So they are literally inexpressable. When we say murder is wrong, we are not describing a fact about murder the way murder causes death describes a fact. Ethics lies outside the world of facts in the realm of value which language cannot capture. This does not make ethics unimportant. Vitkinstein emphasized it makes ethics too important for words. Metaphysics, questions about the ultimate nature of reality, about substances and essences, about what exists beyond experience, all nonsense. Such questions try to say what can only be shown. Philosophy itself, if philosophy's job was to answer these questions, then philosophy has no job. The proper task of philosophy, Vitkinstein concluded, is clarification. Philosophy should show that most philosophical problems arise from misunderstanding our language. The book ends with one of the most famous sentences in philosophy. What we cannot speak about, we must pass over in silence. This was not anti-mystical. Vidkinstein deeply believed in the mystical, the ethical, the aesthetic. He just thought these realms transcended language. Trying to speak about them produces only confusion. Now, let me show you why this theory seemed irresistible to many brilliant minds. The logical positivists of the Vienna circle seized on the tractatus with enthusiasm. Thinkers like Moritz Schlick and Rudolph Carnap saw in Vitkinstein's work a way to finally put philosophy on scientific footing. They developed what they called the verification principle. A statement is meaningful only if it can be verified empirically or is true by definition. Everything else including theology and metaphysics is meaningless. Bertrren Russell, one of the 20th century's greatest logicians, wrote the introduction to the tractus. He recognized its brilliance, even while disagreeing with parts of it. Russell saw that Vitkinstein had pushed logical analysis further than anyone, showing how complex propositions break down into simple ones that directly picture reality. The theory also seemed to explain something puzzling. Why mathematical truths feel necessary. Vitkinstein argued that mathematical propositions are tortologies true by virtue of their logical form alone. 2 + 2 = 4 does not picture any fact about the world. It is a transformation showing that different symbols express the same thing. Mathematics says nothing about reality but shows the logical scaffolding underlying all saying. But even as the tractatus gained influence, problems emerged and Vitkinstein himself began to see them. Here is the first major problem and it is devastating. The tractatus itself violates its own criteria for meaningfulness. The book makes claims about the relationship between language and reality, about logical form, about what can and cannot be said. But by its own logic, these claims do not picture possible states of affairs. They try to say what can only be shown. Vitkinstein knew this. He called his own sentences elucidatory. He compared them to a ladder you climb and then throw away once you have ascended. You use the nonsensical sentences to see clearly then recognize them as nonsense. But this is deeply unsatisfying. How can nonsense elucidate anything? How do we know which nonsense to take seriously and which to dismiss? The second problem concerns the nature of elementary propositions. Vitkinstein argued that all complex propositions break down into elementary ones that directly picture atomic facts, but he never gave a clear example of an elementary proposition. When pressed, he couldn't say what counts as truly atomic. Is the cat is on the mat elementary or does it break down further into propositions about molecular structures and spatial coordinates? This was not a minor technical detail. It struck at the foundation of the theory. If we cannot identify what counts as elementary, how do we know the picture theory applies? How do we know language has the structure Vitkinstein described? Third, the picture theory seems to work well for certain sentences but fails for others. The cat is on the mat seems to picture a state of affairs. But what about there are no elephants in this room. Negative facts are strange. What state of affairs does a negative sentence picture? The absence of something. But absences do not seem to be facts in the world the way presences are. Or consider general statements like all cats are mammals. This does not picture a single state of affairs but ranges over potentially infinite cases. How does the logical form of this sentence correspond to reality or probability statements? It will probably rain tomorrow. What possible state of affairs does this picture? It is not definitely raining or definitely not raining in the picture. Fourth, and this troubled Vitkinstein deeply, the theory seemed to drain language of human meaning. Real language is rich with metaphor, emotion, social context, ambiguity. We comfort, promise, joke, threaten, question, command. The picture theory seemed to capture only one thin slice of language, factual description. It left out almost everything that makes language meaningful to humans. Here is a concrete example that shows this problem. Consider Shakespeare's line, all the worlds a stage. By the picture theory, this is either nonsense or it is a false empirical claim. The world is not literally a stage with curtains and actors. But clearly this metaphor is deeply meaningful. It expresses something profound about the human condition, about performance and authenticity, about life's theatrical quality. Vitkinstein's early philosophy had no room for this kind of meaning. It could not explain why poetry moves us, why religious language matters to believers, why legal language shapes social reality. The debates among scholars about the tractatus remain fierce. Some interpreters call them the austere readers argue that Vitkinstein meant the ladder metaphor literally. The tractatus is deliberately nonsense designed to show the limits of sense. Once you see clearly, you throw away the whole book including its positive doctrines. Philosophy ends not in theories but in silence. Others the substantial readers argue that the tractatus advances real claims about language and reality. The book is not mere therapy but systematic philosophy. The picture theory is a genuine theory we should evaluate on its merits. This debate matters because it shapes how we read Vitkinstein's later work. Did he abandon a failed theory? Or did he abandon the very idea that philosophy should produce theories? There is also fierce debate about what influenced the tractatus. Was Vitkinstein primarily influenced by Russell's logical atomism, by Frager's philosophy of language, by Schopenhau's metaphysics, by Toltoy's religious writings? Each reading yields a different victinstein. Let me give you the most charitable understanding of what the tractatus achieved before Vitkinstein himself rejected it. The book showed perhaps more clearly than any work before it that many philosophical problems arise from confusion about language. Not all philosophical problems, but many. It demonstrated that clarifying what we mean, getting clear about the logical structure of our claims, can dissolve rather than solve certain puzzles. The tractus also articulated a powerful idea. Language has limits and recognizing these limits is itself philosophically important. There are things we cannot say and trying to say them produces only confusion. This does not make those things unreal or unimportant. Most importantly, the tractatus established that understanding language is central to understanding thought and reality. Philosophy cannot proceed without examining its own medium. This insight shaped 20th century philosophy more than any other single idea. But Vitkinstein himself came to see the tractus as fundamentally misguided. Not wrong in its details, but wrong in its entire approach. And that realization led to his second even more revolutionary philosophy. a philosophy that did not just reject the picture theory but rejected the whole idea of building philosophical theories. To understand that transformation, we need to see what happened to Vidgenstein after the tractatus. He thought he had solved philosophy. So he gave it up. He became an elementary school teacher in rural Austria, a gardener at a monastery, an architect. He lived simply, gave away his inherited fortune, sought a life of practical work. But philosophy pulled him back. In the early 1930s, he returned to Cambridge and began teaching. His students noticed something remarkable. He was teaching against his own earlier work. He was not refining the tractatus, but dismantling it piece by piece. And what emerged was not a new theory to replace the old one. It was a radically different way of doing philosophy altogether. One that would prove even more influential and even more controversial than his first revolution. Part two, the return to philosophy. What changed Vitkinstein's mind? For nearly a decade after publishing the tractatus, Vitkinstein stayed away from philosophy. He truly believed he had finished the subject. So what brought him back and more importantly what made him realize his entire first philosophy was wrong. The story begins with conversations. In 1927, Vitkinstein started attending meetings of the Vienna Circle. that group of philosophers and scientists who had embraced his tractus. But something strange happened. As they discussed his work, explaining what they thought he meant, Vitkinstein grew increasingly uncomfortable. The Vienna circle wanted to use the tractatus to eliminate metaphysics and build a scientific worldview. They loved the idea that meaningful statements must be verifiable. But Vitkinstein had never said quite that. He had said some things cannot be said, but he insisted they were still deeply important. The mystical, the ethical, the aesthetic. The Vienna Circle treated these as simply meaningless, not worth discussing. This misunderstanding started a process of self-examination. Had he really meant what they thought he meant? Was the picture theory actually correct? But the real catalyst came from an unexpected source, a conversation with the Italian economist Pierro Srafa. Srafa made a Neapolitan gesture, brushing his chin with his fingertips outward. a gesture meaning something like I couldn't care less or what's it to you then Strafer asked Vitkinstein what is the logical form of that this simple question shattered the tractatus the gesture clearly has meaning anyone who understands Italian culture knows what it communicates but what state of affairs does it picture What is its logical form that corresponds to reality? The gesture does not describe or represent anything the way the cat is on the mat does. It performs a social act. It expresses an attitude. It does something in the world rather than picturing something about the world. Vitkinstein realized that most of our language works more like Srafer's gesture than like simple declarative sentences. We do not just describe reality. We warn, promise, command, question, joke, insult, comfort, threaten, marry, christen ships, declare war, and countless other acts. The picture theory could not account for any of this. Around the same time, another problem emerged from his teaching. In Cambridge, Vitkinstein began working with students on actual examples of how we use words. He asked them to consider ordinary language in ordinary contexts and a pattern emerged. Words do not have single fixed meanings that picture reality. They have families of related uses that shift with context. Take the word game. What is the essence of a game that makes something a game? Is it competition? But solitaire has no competition. Is it winning and losing? But when a child throws a ball against a wall for fun, there is no winning or losing. Is it following rules? But children making up a game as they go are still playing a game. Is it entertainment? But professional chess players work at their games. There is no single feature common to everything we call a game. Instead, there are overlapping similarities, what Vitkinstein came to call family resemblances. Just as members of a family might share various features, some having the same nose, others the same eyes, others the same walk, but no single feature common to all. Words apply to things that share various overlapping similarities without any essential core. This destroyed the tractatus assumption that words must have precise meanings corresponding to reality. language is messier, more flexible, more context dependent than he had thought. A third realization came from watching children learn language. The tractatus assumed that for language to work, there must be a logical connection between words and reality, that somehow the structure of language mirrors the structure of the world. But children do not learn language by being taught logical forms. They learn by being trained in practices. A parent points to a dog and says, "Dog." The child learns to use the word dog not by grasping its logical form, but by participating in activities, by hearing it used in contexts, by being corrected when they use it wrong, by seeing reactions when they use it right. Language is learned as we learn to walk or eat with utensils through immersion in a form of life. This led Vidgenstein to a radical conclusion. Meaning is not correspondence to reality. Meaning is use. Let me unpack what this means because it is the cornerstone of his later philosophy. When we ask what does this word mean? We are really asking how is this word used? The meaning of dog is not some abstract dog essence or even the set of all dogs. The meaning is the role the word plays in our language, the practices and contexts in which we deploy it. Consider the word pain. The early Vitkinstein might have thought pain gets its meaning by picturing an internal state, a mental event of hurting. But the later Vitkinstein asked, "How do we actually use the word pain?" Children learn pain by being taught to replace crying with words. When they fall and cry, adults say, "Does it hurt?" and teach them to respond. We use pain to request help, to explain behavior, to gain sympathy, to describe sensations, to diagnose medical conditions. The word is woven into practices of comforting, treating, and understanding each other. Now this sounds simple but it has explosive consequences. If meaning is used then there is no single correct meaning floating in some abstract realm. There is no essence of meaning independent of how we use words. Different communities can use words differently and both be correct within their practices. Vitkinstein also realized that he had been bewitched by an overly simple model of how language works. He had assumed all meaningful language works like names and descriptions. This made sense for the cat is on the mat, but it made philosophy blind to the incredible variety of what we do with words. He began to see philosophical problems themselves differently. In the tractatus, he thought philosophical problems arose from trying to say the unsayable. Now he saw them arising from something else, from language going on holiday. What does this mean? When we do philosophy, we take words out of their ordinary contexts where their use is clear. We ask abstract questions like what is time or what is knowledge or what is the self? These words work perfectly well in everyday life. We know what it means to be on time, to know your neighbor's name, to find yourself in a mirror. But when we strip away the context and ask these grand questions, the words spin freely, no longer tethered to practices that give them meaning. The philosophical problems are not deep mysteries about reality. They are confusions about language that arise when we forget how words actually function. Let me give you a concrete example that Vitkinstein used himself. Philosophers have long debated what is time? Augustine famously said, "If no one asks me, I know what time is. But if I'm asked to explain it, I do not know. This puzzlement has generated thousands of pages of philosophy. But Vitkinstein would ask, when does the word time actually confuse us in ordinary life? Almost never. We know what it means to be on time, to waste time, to have a good time, to time a race. The word works perfectly in its home contexts. Confusion arises only when we ask the abstract question stripped of context. But what is time really? The question itself creates the confusion. We are looking for an essence, a deep truth about time's nature. But there may be no such thing to find. There are just the various ways we use the word time in our practices. The philosophical problem dissolves when we look at actual use. This new approach led Vitkinstein to abandon the idea of creating a theory. The tractatus was a theory. Language pictures reality. Here is how it works. Here are the consequences. But theories, he now thought, are precisely what philosophy should avoid. Why? Because reality is too diverse. Language is too flexible and life is too complex for any theory to capture. Every theory oversimplifies. Every theory forces reality into a mold. What philosophy should do instead is describe. Look at how language actually works in diverse contexts. Notice patterns. remind ourselves of what we already know but tend to forget when doing philosophy. This was not a retreat to mere description. It was based on a deep conviction. Philosophical problems do not require new information or better theories. They require clearer vision of what is already before us. Imagine someone confused about how chess works asking, "But what is a knight really?" You would not give them a theory of knight essence. You would show them how the knight moves, what role it plays in the game, how it differs from other pieces. You would describe its use. Confusion would clear not by discovering night nature, but by clear description of night function. Vitkinstein saw all philosophical confusion working this way. Now this transformation was not sudden. It happened gradually through the late 1920s and early 1930s. Vitkinstein returned to Cambridge in 1929, submitted the tractatus as his doctoral thesis, though it had been published eight years earlier, and began teaching. His teaching style was remarkable and unlike anything in academic philosophy. He did not lecture from notes. He thought out loud, worked through problems with students, often fell silent for long periods, wrestled visibly with ideas. He made students feel they were witnessing philosophy being done rather than hearing finished results. During these years, he covered his blackboard with examples, ordinary cases of language use, asking students to notice what actually happens when we speak. These discussions formed the basis of what would eventually become his second master work, philosophical investigations, published after his death in 1953. But the transition was painful. Vitkinstein wrote in the preface to philosophical investigations that he had to acknowledge grave mistakes in his earlier work. For someone who had thought he solved philosophy, admitting his system was fundamentally wrong required intellectual courage few philosophers possess. The change also isolated him. The Vienna circle felt betrayed when he rejected their interpretation of his work. Traditional philosophers found his new approach too unsistatic, too focused on ordinary language, not rigorous enough. Even students who loved the tractatus sometimes felt lost when he turned against it. Yet Vitkinstein pressed on because he believed something important was at stake. Philosophy had gone wrong by trying to be like science, seeking theories and explanations. But philosophy's job is not to explain but to clarify, not to discover but to remind, not to theorize, but to dissolve confusion. There is a beautiful metaphor Vitkinstein used for this new conception of philosophy. Philosophy should be like showing a fly the way out of the fly bottle. The fly is trapped, buzzing against the glass, unable to escape. But the bottle is open at one end. The fly does not need new information or a theory of bottle nature. It needs to see what is already there to be shown the obvious exit it keeps missing. We are like that fly when we do philosophy. We are trapped in confusions, buzzing against problems that seem deep and intractable. But often the way out is simple. Look at how we actually use words. Remember the contexts that give them meaning. See the obvious we have overlooked. This approach would soon produce some of the most powerful arguments in 20th century philosophy. Arguments that challenged how we think about mind, meaning, knowledge, and reality itself. Arguments that still divide philosophers today. But before we get to those arguments, we need to understand the full picture of how this later philosophy works. We need to see language games, the concept that replaced the picture theory as the key to understanding language. Part three, language games and meaning as use. The revolutionary turn. If the picture theory was Vitkinstein's first revolution, the concept of language games was his second. And in many ways, it was even more radical. The philosophical investigations opens with a quote from Augustine describing how he learned language as a child. Augustine says, "Aults would point to things and say words, and he learned that each word names a thing. This seems natural, obvious even. But Vidkinstein saw in this apparently innocent description a deeply misleading picture of how language works. Augustine's account assumes language is primarily about naming and describing that words are tags we attach to objects and concepts. This picture, Vitinstein argued, bewitches us into misunderstanding almost everything about language. To break this spell, Vitkinstein introduced one of his most famous concepts, language games. The term is deceptively playful. But Vickinstein was not suggesting language is trivial or that we are just playing around. He chose the word game deliberately because games have certain features that help us understand language. First, games have rules, but these rules are not based on some deep logical necessity. They are conventions we adopt. In chess, bishops move diagonally. Why? There is no reason in the nature of bishops or diagonals. It is simply the rule of the game. Similarly, words have conventional uses not because they must correspond to reality in a certain way, but because these are the practices we have adopted. Second, we learn games by playing them, not by studying theories of games. A child learns chess not by first understanding game theory, but by moving pieces and being corrected. Similarly, we learn language by participating in language games, by using words in social practices. Third, there are many different games with different purposes and different rules. Chess, poker, football, solitire, ring around the rosie. These are all games, but they work completely differently. Similarly, language consists of many different language games with different purposes and different rules. Now, let me show you what a language game is with Vitkinstein's own examples. Imagine a simple scenario. A builder and an assistant are constructing a building. The builder calls out slab and the assistant brings a slab. The builder calls block and the assistant brings a block. The builder calls pillar and the assistant brings a pillar. This is a complete language game. It is primitive but it is genuinely linguistic. The words have meaning not because they picture reality, not because they name essences, but because they function in a practice. The assistant knows what slab means because he knows what to do when he hears it. Now expand this. The builder adds number words, two slabs, then color words, red block, then words like there while pointing. Each addition makes the language game more complex, but the principle remains the same. Words mean what they do in the game. But notice something crucial. There is no single thing called meaning that all these words share. Slab functions as a command or request. Two specifies quantity. Red describes a property. There indicates location. Each plays a different role in the practice. This is what Vitkinstein meant by meaning is use. The meaning of a word is not an object it names or a concept it expresses or a picture it corresponds to. The meaning is the role the word plays in the language game. What we do with it, how we use it in our practices. Let me give you a more complex example to show the power of this idea. Consider the word know. Traditional epistemology asks what is knowledge? What distinguishes knowledge from mere belief? Philosophers have debated for millennia whether knowledge requires certainty. What justification means? How we can know anything about the external world. But Vitkinstein would say, "Look at how we actually use no in different language games." I know how to ride a bicycle means I have a practical skill. Test me by watching me ride. I know it is raining means I can see or hear the rain. My knowledge is based on perception. I know 2 + 2 = 4 means I have mastered a mathematical rule. The question of how I know makes no sense here. I just know because I understand mathematics. I know Paris is in France means I have learned a geographical fact. I might have learned it from maps, books or travel. I know he is in pain means I see his behavior and respond appropriately. I do not infer an inner state from outer signs. I simply see the pain in his face and actions. Each use of no functions differently. There is no single essence of knowledge underlying all these cases. There are family resemblances, overlapping similarities, but no common feature. The philosophical question, what is knowledge really? Arises from thinking there must be a single thing called knowledge, but there is not. There are just diverse uses of the word no in diverse practices. This approach revolutionized how philosophers could address traditional problems. Let me show you with one of philosophy's oldest puzzles. Skepticism about other minds. The problem goes like this. I know I have sensations, thoughts, and feelings because I experience them directly. But I can never experience your sensations, thoughts, and feelings. I only see your behavior. So how can I know you are not a sophisticated robot or philosophical zombie acting conscious but actually empty inside? Deart worried about this. Many philosophers have tried to solve it with arguments by analogy. I see you behaving like I do when I am in pain. So you probably feel pain too. But this seems weak. The analogy is based on a single case myself and generalized to everyone else. Vitkinstein dissolved the problem rather than solving it. Look at the language game we play with psychological words. When do we teach a child the word pain? We do not teach them to name a private inner sensation. We teach them to replace natural expressions of pain like crying with learned expressions like saying it hurts. We say, "Does it hurt when they fall?" We teach them to tell us when they are hurt so we can help. The word pain gets its meaning from being woven into these social practices of responding to injury, seeking comfort, explaining behavior, getting treatment. Now, here is the key point. For this language game to work, there cannot be doubt about whether others feel pain. The language game presupposes that others feel pain. If we really doubted it, we could not teach the word because there would be no reason to ask, "Does it hurt?" or say, "I am sorry that hurt." The skeptical question, "How do I know others have minds?" tries to introduce doubt into a context where doubt makes no sense. It is like asking in the middle of a chess game, "But how do I know we are really playing chess?" The question undermines the very practice that gives the question its terms. This does not mean soypism is false in some traditional philosophical sense. It means the skeptical question is malformed. It arises from taking psychological language out of the language games that give it meaning and treating it as describing hidden inner objects that might or might not exist. Now this approach has a powerful consequence. There are as many language games as there are activities humans engage in with words. We play language games when we give orders and obey them. When we describe objects by appearance or measurements. When we construct an object from a description. When we report events. When we speculate about events. When we form and test hypotheses, when we present results in tables and diagrams, when we make up stories and read them, when we act in plays, when we sing songs, when we guess riddles, when we make jokes and tell them, when we solve problems in arithmetic, when we translate from one language to another, when we ask, thank curse, greet, pray. This is just a small sample. The list is open-ended because human practices are open-ended. New language games can be invented as new activities arise. The language game of computer programming did not exist 300 years ago. The language game of texting with abbreviations and emojis is even newer. Each language game has its own standards of correctness, its own purposes, its own rules. What counts as correct in the language game of giving scientific explanations differs from what counts as correct in the language game of telling jokes. In science, we value literal truth and precision. In jokes, we value surprise, timing, and humor, sometimes at the expense of literal truth. This leads to a crucial insight. There is no universal standard of meaning that applies across all language games. The mistake of many philosophers, including the early Vitkinstein, was to think there must be one correct way language relates to reality. But language relates to reality in as many ways as there are language games. Let me show you how this applies to a contemporary debate, the meaning of religious language. Traditional debates ask are religious statements like God exists true or false? Atheists say false, theists say true. And everyone assumes they are debating factual claims about reality like electrons exist or unicorns do not exist. But Vitkinstein suggests religious language might be playing a different language game entirely. When a believer says God loves me, they might not be making a factual claim about an invisible being's emotional state. They might be expressing trust, orienting their life, finding meaning in suffering, committing to certain values. Religious language might function more like I promise to be faithful than like there are nine planets. A promise is not true or false. It is kept or broken. It performs an action rather than describing a state of affairs. This does not make religious language meaningless or reduce it to mere emotion. It has meaning in the language game believers play in their practices of worship, prayer, ethical living, communal identity. Asking whether religious claims are literally true might be like asking whether a chess move is true, it misunderstands the game being played. Now this interpretation of Vitkinstein on religion is controversial and we will return to it but it shows how the language game concept opens new ways of understanding diverse discourses. However, and this is critical, Vitkinstein was not a relativist. He did not think that because there are many language games anything goes. Each language game has internal standards of correctness. In the builder's language game, if the assistant brings a block when the builder says slab, the assistant is wrong. Not wrong according to some external standard, but wrong within the game they are playing. The rules of the game determine correctness. Similarly, in the language game of giving scientific explanations, there are standards, empirical evidence, logical consistency, predictive power. Someone who violates these standards is not just playing a different game. They are playing the scientific game incorrectly. But here is where it gets complicated. What if someone rejects the scientific language game altogether? What if they say, "I am not playing your game of empirical evidence. I am playing the game of intuition and mystical insight." Vitkinstein's answer seems to be then we cannot argue because argument presupposes a shared game. At some point justification comes to an end and we can only say this is what we do. There are bedrock practices, ways of acting and speaking that are not justified by anything deeper. They are simply our form of life. This introduces one of Vitkinstein's most important and controversial concepts, forms of life. A form of life is the broader context in which language games are embedded. It includes not just linguistic practices but ways of acting, valuing, responding, living. Language games are woven into forms of life the way individual moves are woven into a game. For example, the language game of promising makes sense only within a form of life, where people recognize obligations, where there is a future people plan for, where social cooperation matters. Creatures without these features could not have the practice of promising, even if they made promise-like sounds. Forms of life are not chosen or justified. We are born into them, trained into them, and they form the unquestioned background of our practices. When Vitkinstein says, "If a lion could speak, we could not understand him," he means that a lion's form of life is so different from ours that even if it made sounds, we could not grasp what those sounds meant because meaning depends on shared practices embedded in a form of life. This is deep and unsettling. It suggests that at the foundation of our language and thought, there is no rational justification, no logical necessity. There is just what we do, our form of life, which is given, not justified. Now, let me show you the problems and criticisms this view faces because they are serious. First, if meaning is just used in language games, how do we explain misunderstanding? When two people use a word differently, are they just playing different language games, both correct within their games, or is one of them wrong? Consider a concrete case. A child says, "I know there is a monster under my bed." An adult says, "You do not know. You just believe or imagine. Are they playing different language games with no or is the child using no incorrectly? If they are playing different games, then the adult cannot correct the child. Just introduce them to a new game. But surely the adult is doing more than that. They are teaching the child what no really means. This suggests there is a standard beyond individual games. Second, the language game approach seems to make philosophy impossible. If philosophy's job is to describe language games, not evaluate them, then how can we ever say a language game is confused or problematic? Consider the language game of astrology. People say Mercury is in retrograde. So be careful with communication. They use this language in practices of interpreting events, making decisions, finding meaning. Is Vitkinstein committed to saying astrology is fine within its own game? Many philosophers argue Vitkinstein's approach is too conservative, too accepting of existing practices. It cannot criticize only describe. But surely philosophy should be able to say some practices are based on confusion or error. Third, how do we identify language games? Where does one game end and another begin? Are all uses of no part of one big knowledge language game or are there hundreds of separate knowledge games? Vitkinstein never gave a clear criterion for individuating language games. This makes the concept frustratingly vague. It is a useful metaphor, but is it a rigorous philosophical tool? Fourth, and this is perhaps the deepest problem, the language game approach seems to make meaning too social and conventional. What about individual creativity? novel uses of language, poetry that breaks rules. When Shakespeare writes the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, he is not following established use. He is creating new meaning. How does Vitkinstein account for this? If meaning is just use and use is social practice, where does linguistic innovation come from? Some defenders of Vitkinstein argue he can handle these cases. Language games are flexible and evolve. Novel uses build on existing practices by extending them in new ways. Shakespeare's metaphor works because we already understand slings, arrows, fortune, and outrage, and we can see the creative connection. But critics respond that this still makes individual creativity derivative of social practice when it seems to be something more fundamental. Fifth, there is a worry about relativism. If each language game has its own standards and forms of life are ultimate, how can we ever say one form of life is better than another? Consider a culture with a practice of human sacrifice. Within their language, game and form of life, the practice makes sense, has meaning, serves purposes. Can Vitkinstein say it is wrong? Or must he say it is correct within their form of life? Vitkinstein himself seemed troubled by this. He clearly thought some things were right and others wrong. He lived an intensely ethical life, giving away his fortune, refusing academic honors, seeking truth with painful honesty. But his philosophy seems to undermine the possibility of cross-cultural ethical judgment. His response, as far as we can tell from scattered remarks, was that he was not doing ethics, but describing how language works. Ethics is lived, not theorized. But this response feels evasive to many critics. Sixth, scholars debate whether Vitkinstein's later philosophy is truly non- theoretical. He claimed to offer no theories, only descriptions. But is not the language game concept itself a theory of meaning? Is not meaning is use a theoretical claim? Some interpreters argue Vitkinstein's methodology was self undermining. He wanted to avoid theories but ended up proposing an alternative theory. Others argue he succeeded in being purely descriptive but then question whether pure description can accomplish what philosophy needs to accomplish. Despite these problems, the language game concept transformed philosophy. It influenced ordinary language philosophy, the movement associated with JL Austin and others at Oxford. They analyzed how words function in ordinary contexts, showing that philosophical puzzles often arise from ignoring these contexts. It influenced speech act theory, the study of how we do things with words, how language performs actions like promising, commanding, declaring. It influenced the philosophy of science with thinkers like Thomas arguing that scientific paradigms are like language games with internal standards that shift when paradigms change. It influenced anthropology, psychology, and linguistics, encouraging attention to how language works in social practices rather than abstract systems. Most importantly, it changed what questions philosophers ask. Instead of what is the essence of X, philosophers now ask how do we use the word X in different contexts. Instead of seeking definitions, they seek descriptions of practice. Instead of building theories, they clarify confusions. But the language game concept was just one part of Vitkinstein's later philosophy. He developed a series of arguments that challenged fundamental assumptions about mind, meaning, and knowledge. The most famous and controversial of these was the private language argument. An argument so subtle and complex that philosophers still cannot agree on what it says or whether it works. Part four, the private language argument. Why you cannot have your own language? Imagine you invent a language that only you can understand. You have a sensation, let us say a particular kind of pain, and you decide to call it S. Every time you have this exact sensation, you write S in a diary. No one else knows what S means because no one else can feel your private sensation. This is your private language. Most of us think this is not just possible but obviously true. We have private thoughts, private feelings, private experiences that others cannot directly access. Why couldn't we have private words for them? Vitkinstein argued this is impossible. The private language argument found in sections 243 through 315 of philosophical investigations claims that a language understandable by only one person is incoherent. And this argument, if successful, demolishes huge portions of philosophy and common sense. Let me build the argument carefully, then show you why it matters so much, then examine whether it actually works. The argument starts with a simple question. What makes s meaningful? What makes it the case that when you write S, you are using the symbol correctly or incorrectly? Your first answer might be S means whatever sensation I'm having right now. When I first define it, I create a mental connection between the symbol and the sensation. Later when I use S again, I compare my current sensation to the memory of that original sensation. If they match, I am using S correctly. If they do not, I am using it incorrectly. This seems straightforward, but Vitkinstein saw a devastating problem. How do you know you are remembering the original sensation correctly? You might say, "I just check my memory." But memories can be wrong. Maybe your memory has shifted and what you now remember as the original sensation is not what you actually felt. You might respond, but I know when my memory is reliable, but how what is your standard for checking whether your memory of the sensation is accurate? Here is the problem. In a public language, we can check our memories against external standards. If I am not sure whether I am remembering the word cat correctly, I can ask others, check dictionaries, observe what people call cats. There is a public practice that determines correctness. But in your private language, there is no external standard. You cannot ask anyone else whether you are using S correctly because no one else knows what S means. You cannot compare your use to any public practice. All you have is your impression that you are using it the same way. Your memory of the original sensation. But now comes the crucial move. If there is no external standard, no way to check whether you are right, then the distinction between using s correctly and merely thinking you're using it correctly collapses. Whatever seems right to you is right. But when whatever seems right is right, there is no such thing as right anymore. Vitkinstein puts it this way. One would like to say whatever is going to seem right to me is right. And that only means that here we cannot talk about right. Think about what this means. For a word to have meaning, there must be a distinction between correct and incorrect use. In chess, a move is legal or illegal according to the rules. Without rules, there is no such thing as a legal or illegal move. There is just moving pieces around. Similarly, without a standard for correct use independent of your impression of correctness, S has no meaning. You are not really following a rule when you use S. You just think you are. But thinking you are following a rule is not the same as actually following one. Let me make this concrete with one of Vitkinstein's examples. Imagine you want to know what time a train leaves. You look at a timetable in your imagination. Whatever time you imagine is the time the train leaves according to your imagined timetable. But this is not really consulting a timetable. A real timetable can surprise you, tell you something you did not expect, be right when you thought it was wrong. An imagined timetable just confirms whatever you imagine. Your memory of the original sensation is like an imagined timetable. It cannot serve as a standard because it changes to fit what you think it should be. There is no difference between correctly remembering the sensation and merely thinking you remember it correctly. Now this argument has immediate and radical consequences. First it challenges Carteesian philosophy. Deart built his entire system on the certainty of his own mental states. I think therefore I am. My own thoughts and sensations are what I know most directly and certainly. Everything else could be an illusion. But I cannot doubt my own pain, my own thoughts. But Vitkinstein's argument suggests this is backward. We do not learn language by naming private experiences and then extending it to public things. We learn language through public practices and only then can we apply it to our private experiences. When you learn the word pain, you do not learn it by introspecting a private sensation and attaching a label. You learn it by being trained to replace crying with words, to tell others when you are hurt, to respond to others pain. The meaning of pain is constituted by these public practices. Second, it challenges the idea of private mental objects. We commonly think of thoughts, sensations, and feelings as private objects in an inner mental space that only we can access. The private language argument suggests this picture is confused. There are no private mental objects that we name with words. Rather, psychological language gets its meaning from its role in our public practices of interacting with others, explaining behavior, expressing feelings, seeking help. Third, it challenges theories of meaning based on mental content. Many philosophers think words get their meaning by being associated with mental contents, ideas or concepts in the mind.
